summary: Gives operational guidance on running anycast services, where the same address is announced from several places for resilience and load spreading. It covers practices as services with high availability needs have grown. This is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: If many shops share one phone number and your call goes to the closest, that is anycast. This note gives tips for running it so customers get an answer even if one shop closes.

questions: is anycast good for tcp services
subtitle: Best practice for running a service from many places at once under the same IP address.

tldr.problem: Services with high availability needs want redundancy and load spreading, but running one service from several sites raises routing, monitoring and security pitfalls.
tldr.mechanism: Anycast gives a service a stable set of IP addresses and advertises them in a routing system from two or more independent nodes, so the routing system picks which node answers each client. The RFC lays out design and operating guidance for doing this over an IGP or BGP.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice for operators. It does not say which services should use anycast, and it warns that the approach does not scale as a general method for the global Internet.

today: RFC 4786 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 126) from December 2006. The metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Anycast Is and Who This Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4786 is written for network operators who are weighing whether to run a distributed service using anycast. It describes best current practice but does not recommend whether any particular service should or should not be anycast.

The idea is simple. A service is tied to a stable set of IP addresses, and reachability to those addresses is advertised in a routing system from multiple, independent service nodes. The routing system, not the client, decides which node handles each request. The text applies to both IPv4 and IPv6.

The RFC notes that anycast has become popular for adding redundancy to DNS servers, including several root DNS server operators. It also warns that anycast limits the kind of service you can spread this way, because of transaction longevity, state held on servers and data synchronisation. Monitoring also gets harder, since availability depends on where the client sits in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Anycast means many helpers answer to the same name, and the road system sends you to one of them. This note is a guide for the people who run the helpers.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
A Service Address is the IP address tied to a service. Anycast is making that address available in multiple, discrete, autonomous locations, so datagrams are routed to one of several available locations.

An Anycast Node is an internally-connected collection of hosts and routers that serves the address. To the routing system, each node presents a unique path to the Service Address, and the whole anycast system has two or more nodes. A catchment is the topological region of a network whose packets are routed to one particular node.

Scope matters. A Local-Scope address is visible to only a subset of the routing system and is served by a Local Node. A Global-Scope address is potentially visible to the whole routing system and is served by a Global Node.
sections.plainLanguage: A catchment is the part of the map where all roads lead to the same shop. A local shop only serves its neighbourhood, a global shop can serve anyone.

sections.title: How Anycast Distributes a Service
sections.content:
The service at each node is generally consistent whichever node the routing system picks. No referrals or name-based tricks such as round-robin DNS are required, though they can be combined with anycast. The operator can influence node choice with the traffic engineering features of the routing protocols, to a degree that depends on the scale of the routing system.

Load balancing between nodes is typically difficult and tends to be unbalanced. Spreading load for reliability, and coarse-grained spreading to make popular services scalable, can often be achieved.

The RFC lists common goals: coarse distribution of load, limiting the damage of non-distributed denial-of-service attacks to single nodes, keeping distributed attacks and flash crowds in local regions, helping locate the source of spoofed traffic, faster responses, and reducing many servers to a single distributed address. On response time it is careful: topological nearness does not in general match round-trip performance, so response times may see no reduction and may even increase.

The routing scale can range from a small Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) with a handful of components up to BGP connecting the global Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The map decides which shop you go to, not you. It usually spreads customers a bit unevenly, but it keeps the shops from all being swamped at once.

sections.title: Design Choices: Suitability, Placement and Routing Systems
sections.content:
Because the routing system chooses the node, its choice should stay stable for much longer than a transaction lasts. Single-packet exchanges, such as DNS over UDP, suit anycast well. Long transactions such as bulk downloads and media streaming are harder. For new protocols, the RFC suggests splitting a large transaction into an initialisation phase handled by anycast servers and a sustained phase handled by non-anycast servers. Long flows can also fail in ways more complex than a simple destination unreachable error.

Node placement follows the goals. Examples given are one node per site for an ISP resolver, nodes in regions with poor external connectivity for a root DNS server, and nodes at exchange points for an FTP mirror.

Within an IGP the operator usually controls the whole network, so behaviour is better understood and host routes can be introduced directly. Across the global Internet with BGP, the routing system is generally controlled by other people and BGP practice adds constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Anycast works best for quick questions, like asking the time. For a long chat it is risky, because the road system might switch you to a different shop halfway through.

sections.title: Routing Considerations in Practice
sections.content:
Signalling availability. Once a node advertises the Service Address, packets arrive, so the node must be ready first. Ideally the advertisement is tied to the health of the service: available triggers the route, unavailable triggers a withdrawal. Rapid advertise/withdraw oscillation should be avoided, for example with a minimum delay after a withdrawal.

Covering prefix. In global BGP a host route cannot be relied on to propagate, because of operational policy, so a covering route with a short enough prefix is needed. For IPv4 this is often a 24-bit prefix. Each such route adds scaling cost, and the RFC concludes that these scaling problems prevent anycast from being a useful general approach on the global Internet, though it remains useful for a limited number of Internet-critical services and for smaller networks.

Equal-cost paths. If equal-cost paths lead to different nodes, packets of one transaction may be split, which is a problem for TCP. Per-packet load balancing across links to different neighbour ASes can make the service unavailable to clients downstream of that router.

Route dampening. Flapping routes are dampened as described in RFC 2439, and some implementations penalise by AS_PATH. The RFC advises making AS_PATH attributes from different nodes as diverse as possible, for instance the same origin AS but different upstream ASes.

Other checks. Reverse Path Forwarding checks can wrongly drop packets from multi-homed sites, and a set of Anycast Nodes looks like one, so follow RFC 3704. Local Nodes should restrict propagation with explicit attributes such as NO_EXPORT or NOPEER rather than implicit policy.
sections.plainLanguage: A shop should only put its sign on the road once it is open, and take it down when it closes. It should not flip the sign on and off all the time, or the map makers will start ignoring it.

sections.title: Addressing, Data, Autonomy and Multi-Service Nodes
sections.content:
Addressing. Service Addresses must be unique within the routing system and chosen so that routes propagate. For an IPv4 Internet service, that may mean a block whose minimum RIR allocation is 24 bits and originating the covering 24-bit prefix. In a private network a locally-unused RFC 1918 address may be signalled with a 32-bit host route. IPv6 anycast addresses are not scoped differently from unicast, and the old ban on anycast services over IPv6 was removed from the IPv6 addressing specification in RFC 4291.

Data synchronisation. Nodes should give consistent answers, so data sets need to be synchronised, using examples such as zone transfers for DNS and rsync for FTP archives. This uses non-anycast addresses and, across public networks, should use authentication and encryption.

Node autonomy. To avoid cascading failure, make nodes as self-sufficient as possible, mix Global and Local Nodes, and consider running different operating systems and software. The RFC admits this conflicts with keeping things simple to operate.

Multi-service nodes. When several services share nodes, three approaches are described: multiple covering prefixes, pessimistic withdrawal and intra-node interior connectivity.

Node identification and monitoring. Protocols should include in-band ways to identify the answering node, such as the DNS NSID option or the hostname in an SMTP greeting, and this is strongly recommended. Services should be monitored from probes distributed representatively across the routing system, recording which node answered.
sections.plainLanguage: Every shop needs the same stock list, and shops should not depend on each other to open. It also helps if each reply says which shop answered, so problems are easy to track down.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Anycast can help against denial-of-service attacks. A node can act as a sink for attack traffic from its own sphere of influence, and the work of sorting attack traffic from legitimate traffic is spread over all the nodes.

There are costs. Running many nodes adds monitoring and administration burden, which might reduce host and router security, and taking a compromised server off-line only helps if there are working procedures to do it quickly and reliably.

Service hijacking is the main risk: an unauthorised party might advertise routes for the Service Addresses, capturing requests or handling them in a way that compromises the service. A rogue node can be hard to detect, and because legitimate nodes are visible in the routing system it may be harder to spot. The RFC recommends robust protocols, with strong authentication or integrity protection, for anycast services that need them.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake shop could put up a sign with the same phone number and steal your calls. So the real shops should prove who they are every time they talk to you.
